books.section: Topic 6.12 Controversies over the Role of Government in the Gilded Age
The Silver Issue and the Populist Movement

primary_sources: Frederick Burr Opper, 'The Silver-Tongued Ventriloquist and His Dummies,' Puck, August 12, 1896

stimulus.text: Political cartoon, “The Silver-Tongued Ventriloquist and His Dummies,” by Frederick Burr Opper, Puck, August 12, 1896. A large bearded man wearing a sash labeled “Silver Mine Owner” sits on a box marked “16 to 1.” He holds a small dummy labeled “Bryan” who waves a paper reading “Free Silver Harangues.” At the left, three more small dummies sit in a box, labeled “Tillman,” “Peffer,” and “Altgeld.” At the right, another dummy labeled “Sewall” sits in a box. The caption reads, “If the Show Succeeds, He’ll Get All the Profits.”
stimulus.source_note: Frederick Burr Opper, 'The Silver-Tongued Ventriloquist and His Dummies,' Puck, August 12, 1896. Public domain: cartoon published 1896 (pre-1930); Library of Congress, LCCN2012648552. Labels and caption checked against the image.

stem: What is the cartoonist’s argument about free silver?

options.text: Free silver would help farmers more than anyone else
options.misconception: The caption says the mine owner gets all the profits, not the farmers.

options.text: Free silver would enrich silver mine owners, not farmers
Silver mine owners opposed Bryan and free silver
options.misconception: The mine owner holds Bryan as his dummy, so he supports the silver campaign.

options.text: The cartoon supports free silver as honest reform
options.misconception: The cartoon mocks Bryan as a dummy, so it attacks free silver rather than supporting it.

rationales.A: The caption gives all the profits to the mine owner, not to farmers.
rationales.B: The mine owner works the dummy, and the caption gives him all the profits.
rationales.C: The mine owner holds Bryan as his dummy, so he backs the silver campaign.
rationales.D: Bryan drawn as a dummy is mockery, not support for free silver.
rationales.general:
Read the joke to the end.
1. Bryan is a dummy, and the silver mine owner is the ventriloquist.
2. The dummies wave 'Free Silver Harangues' while the owner sits on '16 to 1.'
3. The caption says that if the show succeeds, the owner gets all the profits.
4. The argument is that free silver serves the mine owners, not the farmers it claims to help.
Remember: a cartoon's caption often states its argument outright.
